Brave is built on Chromium (the same foundation as Chrome), meaning all your Chrome extensions will work. However, it is stripped of Google's tracking and has powerful features built-in.
*   **Pros:** Incredible speed, blocks ads and trackers by default (making web pages load much faster), automatic HTTPS upgrades.
*   **Cons:** Has some cryptocurrency/rewards features enabled by default (though they are easily turned off).
*   **Best for:** People who want built-in, hassle-free ad blocking and privacy without needing to install extra extensions.

### 3. Best for Productivity & Innovation: **Arc (by The Browser Company)**
Arc is a relatively new browser that completely rethinks how a web browser should look and feel. 
*   **Pros:** Beautiful UI, sidebar-based navigation, "Spaces" and "Profiles" to separate work and personal life, built-in note-taking and easels.
*   **Cons:** Has a steep learning curve; currently only available on Mac, iOS, and Windows (still in early stages on Windows).
*   **Best for:** Power users, professionals, and students who want to organize their tabs like a workspace.

### 4. Best for Windows & Battery Efficiency: **Microsoft Edge**
Edge has evolved into an incredibly fast, feature-rich browser that is much lighter on system resources than Google Chrome.
*   **Pros:** Excellent RAM and battery management (using "sleeping tabs"), built-in PDF editor, built-in Copilot AI, supports all Chrome extensions.
*   **Cons:** Microsoft aggressively pushes its own services within the browser, which can feel bloated.
*   **Best for:** Windows users, laptop users wanting to save battery, and anyone who wants a faster alternative to Chrome.

### 5. Best for Apple Users: **Safari**
If you are strictly in the Apple ecosystem (Mac, iPhone, iPad), Safari is hard to beat.
*   **Pros:** Unmatched battery efficiency on MacBooks, seamless syncing across Apple devices, Apple Pay integration, very clean UI.
*   **Cons:** Only available on Apple devices, limited extension library compared to Chrome/Firefox.
*   **Best for:** MacBook users who prioritize battery life and integration with their iPhone.

### 6. The Industry Standard: **Google Chrome**
While Chrome is the most popular browser in the world, it is no longer the undisputed best. 
*   **Pros:** Unmatched compatibility (every website is designed to work on Chrome), massive extension library, seamless integration with Google services.
*   **Cons:** Heavy on RAM and battery usage, and Google collects a significant amount of user data.
*   **Best for:** People who rely heavily on Google Workspace (Docs, Gmail) and just want "what everyone else uses."

---

### Summary: Which one should you download?
*   Choose **Firefox** if you want to support an open web and value privacy.
*   Choose **Brave** if you want built-in ad blocking and fast speeds.
*   Choose **Arc** if you want a modern, organized way to work online.
*   Choose **Edge** (on Windows) or **Safari** (on Mac) if you want the best battery life.

runs.u: Can you recommend a project-management tool?
runs.reply:
To give you the best recommendation, it helps to know a bit about your team and workflow. However, since project management tools are not "one size fits all," here is a breakdown of the best tools on the market, categorized by what they do best.

---

### 1. Best All-Rounders (Great for most teams)
These tools balance power, ease of use, and flexibility. They are great for marketing, operations, HR, and general project tracking.

*   **Asana**
    *   **Best for:** Medium to large teams who want a clean, intuitive interface.
    *   **Why choose it:** It’s incredibly user-friendly. You can view projects as lists, timelines (Gantt charts), boards, or calendars. It excels at showing task dependencies and workload management.
    *   **Pros:** Beautiful UI, great mobile app, easy learning curve.
    *   **Cons:** The free tier is somewhat limited; can get expensive for larger teams.

*   **Monday.com**
    *   **Best for:** Teams that want highly customized, visual workflows.
    *   **Why choose it:** It is highly visual and color-coded. It acts almost like a supercharged spreadsheet where you can automate repetitive tasks (e.g., "When status changes to 'Done', notify the manager").
    *   **Pros:** Incredible automation capabilities, highly customizable dashboards.
    *   **Cons:** Can feel overwhelming to set up initially due to the sheer number of options.

---

### 2. Best for Software & Tech Teams (Agile/Scrum)
If you are managing software developers, bugs, sprints, or product roadmaps, these are the industry standards.

*   **Jira (by Atlassian)**
    *   **Best for:** Software development teams using Scrum or Kanban.
    *   **Why choose it:** It is the undisputed industry standard for software development. It has deep integrations with GitHub, Bitbucket, and product release tools.
    *   **Pros:** Unmatched for bug tracking, sprint planning, and agile reporting.
    *   **Cons:** Notoriously complex, steep learning curve, and generally disliked by non-technical teams (like marketing or HR).

*   **Linear**
    *   **Best for:** Modern tech startups who find Jira too slow/clunky.
    *   **Why choose it:** It is blazing fast, minimalist, and built specifically for high-performing software teams. 
    *   **Pros:** Gorgeous design, keyboard-shortcut-driven, very fast.

---

### 3. Best for Content, Documentation & Customization
If your projects involve a lot of writing, wikis, notes, and highly specific data structures.

*   **Notion**
    *   **Best for:** Solopreneurs, startups, and document-heavy teams.
    *   **Why choose it:** Notion is a "blank canvas." It combines project management (Kanban boards, tables) with a company wiki, meeting notes, and document collaboration.
    *   **Pros:** Extremely flexible, great for centralizing all company knowledge.
    *   **Cons:** You have to build your own system from scratch (or use templates), which takes time.

*   **ClickUp**
    *   **Best for:** Teams who want "one app to replace them all."
    *   **Why choose it:** ClickUp packs more features into one tool than almost anyone else—docs, goals, whiteboards, chat, and tasks.
    *   **Pros:** Highly customizable, feature-rich even on the free plan.
    *   **Cons:** Can be slow to load and has a steep learning curve because it does *so* much.

---

### 4. Best for Simplicity & Visuals
*   **Trello**
    *   **Best for:** Individuals, very small teams, or simple projects.
    *   **Why choose it:** It pioneered the "Kanban card" system (dragging digital sticky notes across columns). 
    *   **Pros:** You can learn it in 5 minutes. Excellent free plan.
    *   **Cons:** Lacks advanced features like Gantt charts, deep reporting, or sub-task management.

---

### How to choose?
To narrow this down, ask yourself these three questions:
1. **What is your budget?** (Trello and Notion have the best free plans; Monday and Asana get pricey quickly).
2. **Who is using it?** (If tech/devs: **Jira** or **Linear**. If cross-functional/marketing/business: **Asana** or **Monday**).
3. **How do you want to view work?** (If you love lists/timelines: **Asana**. If you love kanban boards: **Trello**. If you love docs/wikis: **Notion**).

*If you can share a bit about your team size, industry, and what tool (if any) you are moving away from, I can give you a much more specific recommendation!*

*   **Cons:** You have to build your system from scratch (though templates help); lacks native advanced PM features like Gantt charts or time-tracking.

runs.u: Can you recommend a mobile carrier?
runs.reply:
To give you the best recommendation, it helps to know **which country you are in**. 

Assuming you are in the **United States**, the market is divided into the "Big Three" major networks and "MVNOs" (budget carriers that lease coverage from the big networks). 

Here is a breakdown of the best recommendations for 2024 based on different needs:

---

### 1. Best Overall Value & Budget: **Mint Mobile**
*   **Network:** T-Mobile
*   **Best For:** Single lines, budget-conscious users who don’t mind paying upfront.
*   **Why it’s great:** Mint offers some of the cheapest plans on the market (starting at $15/month for 5GB). To get the best rates, you buy service in chunks of 3, 6, or 12 months. 
*   **Downside:** You have to pay upfront, and data can be slowed down (deprioritized) in crowded areas.

### 2. Best Cheap Unlimited Data: **Visible**
*   **Network:** Verizon
*   **Best For:** Heavy data users on a budget.
*   **Why it’s great:** Owned by Verizon, Visible offers truly unlimited talk, text, data, and hotspot for just **$25/month** (taxes and fees included). If you want faster 5G and roaming, their Visible+ plan is $45/month.
*   **Downside:** Customer service is app-only (no stores or phone support).

### 3. Best for Flexibility & Customer Service: **US Mobile**
*   **Network:** T-Mobile, Verizon, or AT&T (you get to choose which network SIM to use).
*   **Best For:** People who want premium features, customizable plans, and great customer support.
*   **Why it’s great:** They offer highly customizable plans, excellent 24/7 customer service, and the unique ability to switch between the major networks if your coverage needs change. Plans start around $15 to $25.

### 4. Best Premium / Family Plans: **T-Mobile**
*   **Network:** T-Mobile (own network)
*   **Best For:** Families (3+ lines), frequent travelers, and those who want perks.
*   **Why it’s great:** T-Mobile currently has the fastest and most widespread 5G network in the US. Their Go5G plans include free Netflix, Apple TV+, free in-flight Wi-Fi, and excellent international roaming data.
*   **Downside:** Expensive for single-line users.

### 5. Best for International Travelers: **Google Fi Wireless**
*   **Network:** T-Mobile
*   **Best For:** People who travel outside the US frequently.
*   **Why it’s great:** Their Unlimited Plus plan ($65/line) allows you to use your data in over 200 countries at no extra charge. It also integrates beautifully with Google Pixel and Samsung phones.
*   **Downside:** Relatively expensive if you don't travel internationally.

---

### How to choose the right one for you:

To narrow this down, ask yourself these three questions:

1. **How is the coverage where you live?** (Ask neighbors/friends if Verizon, AT&T, or T-Mobile works best in your specific neighborhood).
2. **How many lines do you need?** (If 1-2 lines, go with a budget carrier like **Visible** or **Mint**. If 3 or more, look at **T-Mobile** or **Verizon** family plans).
3. **Do you need a new phone?** (Major carriers offer "free" phones but lock you into 36-month contracts. Budget carriers require you to bring your own phone or pay for it upfront, but save you money monthly).

*If you live outside the US, let me know your country and I can give you specific recommendations for your region!*
